newsitem.title: UK: Cervical treatment prevents cancer, study finds.
newsitem.headline: Cervical treatment prevents cancer, study finds.

text.p: Conservative treatment of women who have pre-cancerous changes in the cervix can protect them from cancer for years, British doctors reported on Friday.
Women have regular Pap smears to check for these changes, which can be treated in a variety of ways ranging from radical hysterectomy to watching and waiting.
The treatment usually depends on the severity of the changes in the cells at the cervix, or the neck of the womb.
Dr Pat Soutter and colleagues at the Royal Postgraduate Medical School at London's Hammersmith Hospital followed up the cases of nearly 45,000 women in four British cities.
More than 2,000 of these showed the changes in their cervical cells known as cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN).

The four centres all used so-called conservative methods of treating the CIN, which include freezing the cervix, using a laser to take away layers of damaged cells, or loop diathermy, a type of heat treatment. Only 33 women developed invasive cancer. Most cases were diagnosed in the first five years after treatment.

Other studies indicate that, untreated, the rate of invasive cervical cancer is about 18 percent in 10 years. So had the 2,116 women with CIN not been treated, 296 would have been expected to develop cancer over the eight-year period of the study.

"These data show that conservative oupatient therapy in women with CIN reduces the risk of invasive cancer of the cervix by 95 percent during the first eight years after treatment, Soutter's group wrote in a report in the Lancet medical journal.

"However, even with careful, long-term follow-up, the risk of invasive cervical cancer among these women is about five times greater than that among the general population during that period. Careful follow-up is essential for at least 10 years after conservative treatment of CIN."
Women who have had unusual smears are urged to have regular checks afterwards, but in Britain this usually only goes on for five years, after which women go back to having smears every three years.
Mitchell Morris of the department of gynaecological oncology at the University of Texas criticised some aspects of Soutter's study but said it provided important information.

"The paper should have a positive impact on both medical paractice and health policy; women who have been treated for preinvasive cervical lesions remain at risk of new lesions, including invasive cancer, for many years after the primary treatment," he wrote in a commentary.
